posts.heading: September 11, 2026
posts.text: The day closes with 107 feeder visits, a figure that remains well above the recent daily average of 33. Carolina Wrens provided a final spurt of detections near sunset, while the wire saw fewer late visitors than the earlier rush.

posts.heading: September 11, 2026
posts.text:
The Ruby-throated Hummingbird holds the feeder's attention in the afternoon, captured in a series of low-resolution frames as it hovers and feeds. Its last confirmed visit occurred thirty-four minutes before this entry, extending the station's activity well beyond the midday peak.

Activity remains significantly above the recent norm, with 95 total visits so far compared to an average of 26.8. The Tufted Titmouse and Carolina Chickadees continue to dominate the wire, their combined presence anchoring the day's higher traffic levels.

The audio backdrop has thinned since the morning rush, with Carolina Wrens and American Crows still registering detections but at lower frequencies than the 9:00 hour peak. The station records 13 species today. The weather holds steady at 30.1 C with light winds.

posts.heading: September 11, 2026
posts.text:
A Tufted Titmouse touched the wire six minutes after sunrise. By 10:30, the station logged 87 visits against a recent average of 19.2, with Titmice and Carolina Chickadees accounting for the bulk of the early activity before Nuthatches joined the mix. Carolina Wrens provided the constant audio backdrop, their 48 detections far outpacing the 35 American Crows and 9 Red-bellied Woodpeckers heard in the canopy.

An American Goldfinch marked the station’s first confident visual record, arriving as the feeder traffic shifted. The day so far shows 13 species compared to the recent daily average of 6.5. Blue Jays and Gray Catbirds appeared briefly, while the wire remained a domain for small songbirds, with the Titmouse returning as late as 197 minutes after sunrise.

posts.heading: September 10, 2026
posts.text:
The day closed with a final burst of auditory activity, as American Crows and Blue Jays dominated the 17:00 and 18:00 hours. This late surge brought the total to 110 feeder visits and 221 auditory detections, figures that remain significantly higher than the recent daily averages of 7.3 and 107.3.

The wire saw its last confirmed visitors in the late afternoon. A Northern Mockingbird arrived at 19:27, marking the final visual record of the day. It was joined by a Carolina Wren, which continued its presence on the wire after its earlier mid-morning visits.

The station concludes its first day of full visual records with 16 species identified. The consistent presence of Tufted Titmice and Carolina Chickadees throughout the day established a steady baseline for the feeder, while the background of crows and wrens filled the air from pre-dawn to dusk.

posts.heading: September 10, 2026
posts.text:
By 15:30, the feeder has logged 102 visits, a volume that stands starkly in contrast to the recent daily average of 1.7. Tufted Titmice and Carolina Chickadees have held the wire in shifts. The auditory log remains dense, with Carolina Wrens accounting for 61 detections and American Crows adding 43 more to the background noise. This is a busier afternoon than the previous day’s midday counts, which totaled only 5 visits.

The station’s visual records are expanding. A Mourning Dove landed at the feeder. These sightings join the earlier confident records of Ruby-throated Hummingbirds and Northern Bobwhites, broadening the list of species confirmed on the wire.

The air is warm at 29.8 C with light winds of 8 kph, and no precipitation has fallen. Blue Jays have become more vocal in the afternoon, with six detections in the 15:00 hour, while Eastern Towhees continue to call from the understory. The Red-shouldered Hawk was last heard in the 12:00 hour. The station has recorded 16 species so far, with 8 of them also heard, marking a significant increase over the 5.3 species average from recent days.

posts.heading: September 10, 2026
posts.text:
The feeder opened its day with a Tufted Titmouse arriving five minutes before sunrise. By 07:16, Carolina Chickadees joined the titmouse on the wire, and by 07:34, a Ruby-throated Hummingbird was already at the feeders. The activity level stands far above the recent average, with 76 visits recorded by 10:30 compared to a baseline of 0.3 on prior days.

While the Carolina Wren dominated the auditory log with 54 detections, the visual record highlights the first confident sightings of a Mourning Dove and a White-breasted Nuthatch at this station. The Nuthatch was observed foraging on a metal pole, displaying its distinctive blue-gray back and thin black eyeline. These two species mark the station's first visual records, adding to the fourteen species counted so far.

The mid-morning brought a flurry of Carolina Chickadee visits between 09:16 and 09:28, interwoven with returning Tufted Titmice. The Red-shouldered Hawk was detected in the 10:00 hour. The steady presence of crows and wrens continues to underscore the shift from the quiet pre-dawn calls to the bustling feeder traffic.

posts.heading: September 9, 2026
posts.text:
The feeder became the center of activity for the final hour at 18:46. Tufted Titmice visited three times in quick succession, joined briefly by a Carolina Chickadee and a Blue Jay. The total count of twenty-two visits stands as the first record for this station.

By 19:19, a Northern Mockingbird arrived to hold the perch until the last confirmed sighting at 19:27. It was joined by a Carolina Wren, which also landed on the feeder for the first time today. The day’s auditory total of two hundred and thirty-eight detections is significantly higher than the recent average of forty-two.

The day’s visual record remains modest, with only two species confirmed with high confidence.

posts.heading: September 9, 2026
posts.text:
The feeder received its first visitors today. A Ruby-throated Hummingbird arrived at 11:44, followed by a Tufted Titmouse at 12:13, and a Gray Catbird at 15:21.

Carolina Wrens have accumulated fifty-seven detections so far, with their most intense burst occurring during the 9:00 hour. Eastern Towhees and Red-bellied Woodpeckers maintain a steady background presence, while American Crows contributed thirty-seven calls, mostly in the early morning.

The weather is mild, with a high of 28.7 C and light wind, and no precipitation has fallen. The visual count stands at three birds. The total detections are forty-six percent higher than yesterday's total at this time.

posts.heading: September 9, 2026
posts.text:
The pre-dawn watch belonged entirely to the Eastern Screech-Owl, which kept the station company with eight calls between midnight and 5:00 AM. By sunrise, the chorus shifted as American Crows flooded in with thirty-three detections during the 7:00 hour, accompanied by a single, brief call from a Red-shouldered Hawk.

As the light strengthened, the Carolina Wren took over the conversation, amassing forty-nine calls by 10:30 AM. Eastern Towhees joined the mix after 8:00, adding twelve detections alongside a lone Red-bellied Woodpecker. No birds landed on the feeder, leaving the visual count at zero.

posts.heading: September 8, 2026
posts.text:
The evening brought a final surge of sound that doubled the day’s total to seventy-nine detections, far exceeding the recent average of five. This late burst was driven by seven Eastern Towhees and four Red-bellied Woodpeckers, marking the first time since the morning that the woodpecker’s knocks returned with such volume. The Carolina Wren added three more calls to the mix, maintaining its steady presence across the day's final hours.

The American Crow, which dominated the start of the day, reappeared with six detections in the 17:00 hour, though it did not feature in the final evening rush. This late-afternoon activity stands in sharp contrast to yesterday, when all recorded sound arrived in a single cluster just before sunset. The station’s log remains strictly auditory, with no visual contacts or feeder visits recorded despite the increased vocal traffic.

As the light fades after the 19:00 hour, the Red-shouldered Hawk’s earlier presence has quieted, leaving the wrens and towhees to close out the day. The day ended with a sustained volume of sound rather than the singular, brief cluster observed in the previous entry. The station’s record reflects a full day of activity, defined entirely by the birds' voices in the absence of any physical interaction with the feeder.

posts.heading: September 8, 2026
posts.text:
The midday hours brought a steady rhythm of sound, with the Carolina Wren and Red-bellied Woodpecker providing the majority of the day’s fifty-two total detections. Unlike the single burst recorded in the morning, activity spread evenly across the hours, including a notable presence of Red-shouldered Hawks in the late morning and early afternoon. The weather remains calm and dry, with no precipitation and light winds, while the feeder itself has seen zero physical visits.

As the afternoon progresses, the auditory count has outpaced recent days, where previous records show no data or minimal activity. The Red-bellied Woodpecker continues to register frequently, appearing in four separate hourly blocks throughout the day. This sustained vocal presence contrasts with the lack of visual confirmation, keeping the station’s record strictly limited to sound.

The log concludes with a final check of the species list, confirming that no new birds have been added to the station’s known roster today. The American Crow’s dominance from the morning has faded, replaced by a more balanced mix of wrens, woodpeckers, and jays. With the light still strong and the feeder untouched, the station maintains its quiet, invisible presence until evening.

posts.heading: September 8, 2026
posts.text:
The morning began with a distinct shift in profile compared to yesterday, as all twenty detections arrived in a single block during the 09:00 hour. This early concentration marks a departure from the late-afternoon clustering observed previously, with American Crows dominating the auditory landscape with ten calls.

The rest of the station’s activity followed the crows, including five Eastern Towhees and two Blue Jays. Red-bellied Woodpeckers added two distinct knocks to the mix, while a single Carolina Wren provided the day's only instance of that species.

With no visual contacts recorded and the feeder remaining untouched, the station’s log rests entirely on this early vocal burst. This marks the first time the station has seen any activity in the morning, breaking the recent pattern of empty ledgers.

posts.heading: September 7, 2026
posts.text:
The day closed with no visual contacts at the feeder, leaving the log to rest entirely on sound. Only two species were detected throughout the period, with the total count remaining quiet at five instances. Since there is no prior data from the recent week, it is difficult to gauge whether this level of activity is typical or exceptional for the station.

All detections arrived in a single cluster during the 19:00 hour, just before sunset. The Carolina Wren accounted for three of the hearing, while the Eastern Towhee provided the remaining two. This late-afternoon concentration meant the earlier hours passed without any recorded activity.

With the light fading and the birds gone, the station ends its first logged day on a hushed note. The lack of feeder visits suggests the birds were moving through the area rather than staying to feed. The log is now closed, awaiting the next day's observations.
